screened.motion: This house believes coding agents make it better to own your core code than to depend on popular frameworks.
screened.why: Both reject the motion: they argue that agents make writing code cheap but not owning it, and that popular frameworks soak up edge-case and maintenance costs a bespoke stack can't, even though Gemini was assigned to argue for it.

screened.motion: This house believes the agent's maker, not the developer, is to blame when a coding agent leaks secrets into a repository.
screened.why: Claude was assigned to argue against, but both agents say the maker carries most of the blame, and both admit developers made smaller mistakes.

screened.motion: This house believes engineers should run coding agents in a minimal harness they control rather than the AI lab's official one.
screened.why: Both agents, whatever side they were given, conclude that most engineers should stay with the official harness and that a minimal one like Pi suits only power users who enjoy maintaining their own tools.

screened.motion: This house believes coding agents should run with the developer's own privileges rather than in a sandbox.
screened.why: Both oppose the motion: each says running agents with full developer privileges is reckless as a default and wants sandboxing or fine-grained capability controls, even though Gemini was assigned to argue for it.

motion: This house believes coding agents make it better to own your core code than to depend on popular frameworks.

claude.en: I mostly held my position, but I moved a little.

alt: The Motion, Motion 10. This house believes coding agents make it better to own your core code than to depend on popular frameworks. Gemini, after arguing for, alone: "Claude called out that contradiction, and they were right—I didn't really believe my own defence there."
